VECTOR: Velocity Based Temperature-field Monitoring with Distributed Acoustic Devices

a temperature-field monitoring system that achieves high temperature sensing accuracy and fast response time using commercial sound playing/recording devices
Haoran Wan1  ·  Lei Wang1  ·  Ting Zhao1  ·  Ke Sun2  ·  Shuyu Shi1  ·  Haipeng Dai1  ·  Guihai Chen1  ·  Haodong Liu3  ·  Wei Wang1

What it is

Real-world use

A car's own speakers and microphones read each seat's air

Imagine a car that keeps each seat comfortable by listening to its own sound system.

Motivation

Temperature sensors read one point, with a delay

  1. 1most temperature sensors only measure the temperature at a single location
  2. 2the wiring and deployment cost could be far more than the sensor hardware
  3. 3While infrared cameras can capture temperature distribution, they are still too expensive for environment monitoring applications.
what each way reads

It shows What each earlier way reads: a probe's slow curve against the air's quick change, then a camera's picture of warm surfaces.

How to read it First the air in grey and the probe's slow reading in colour; then the room's probes from above; then the camera's warm surfaces.

State of the art

Earlier systems read one point or need special hardware

  1. 1each RFID can only measure the temperature at a single location as traditional temperature sensors
  2. 2due to the short distance between speakers and microphones, Acute only measures temperature around the device
  3. 3most of existing systems use specialized and synchronized transceivers
earlier ways: what each reads, what each needs

It shows Earlier ways, by what they read and what they need: few read the air's field, and those need special devices or read it coarsely.

How to read it Right means it reads more places, up to a whole room; up means it needs less, down to the speakers and mics already there.

Background

Four terms used throughout

Speed of sound01

the speed of sound increases by around 0.2% when the air temperature raises by one degree Celsius at room temperature

Time of flight, the travel time02

For a 60 cm path, temperature change of 1 °C at room temperature of 25 °C yields a 3.02 μs difference in ToF

Phase, where the wave is in its cycle03

a phase change of 2π at 19 kHz carrier is equivalent to 52.6 μs in ToF

Temperature field04

temperature distribution monitoring systems provide fine-grained spatial temperature variation information of the target area

the term, drawn

It shows Each term as a picture: the sound's speed, its travel time, the carrier's phase, and a map of temperatures.

How to read it One picture a term; numbers are the paper's (60 cm, 3.02 µs, 19 kHz, 52.6 µs).

Core idea

Sound's travel time gives the air temperature on its path

  1. 1the speed of sound is physically related to the air temperature
  2. 2we can infer the temperature along a given path using the time-of-flight (ToF) measurements
  3. 3we can reconstruct the temperature distribution using line-of-sight (LoS) paths and reflected paths
sound, air and travel time

It shows Warmer air carries sound faster, so a known path's travel time gives its air temperature; many paths give a map.

How to read it Left, the speed of sound against the air temperature; right, the travel time on a 60 cm path, then the car's paths over each seat.

Core idea · what to observe

Warm air on the path shortens the travel time

the speed of acoustic signal is physically determined by the air temperature, which incurs almost no delay

we are actually measuring the temperature’s harmonic mean along the propagation path

  1. Warm air crosses the path: the sound arrives sooner
  2. Off the path, the warm air changes nothing
  3. One degree warmer over 60 cm: 3.02 µs sooner
  4. Your turn Drag the warm air across the path

ToF and temperature

It shows Warm air on the path makes sound faster, so the ToF drops by about 3 µs for each 1 °C.

How to read it Left: the ToF over time, each dot one reading, the line the true value; right: the path's mean temperature.

Core idea · what to observe

The travel time reads the path's average warmth

the ToF along the path is a line integralIn our words: each bit of the path adds its own time, so warm air counts by how long it is on the path and how warm it is.

the weights are the length of the given path passing through the regionIn our words: a warm region counts by the length of the path inside it. In the paper the region is a cell, such as a seat in a car; here it is the warm air.

  1. Warm air twice as long on the path: twice the drop
  2. Half as long but twice as warm: the same drop
  3. Both give the path the same average warmth
  4. Your turn Drag the warm air across the path

Challenge 1 · ToF resolution

A degree moves the travel time far less than one sample

the interval between consecutive samples is 20.8μs, which is far greater than the small change in ToF

  1. One degree warmer: the travel time moves 3 µs
  2. The correlation peak moves in 5.2 µs steps
  3. So its reading jumps between levels 0.9 °C apart
  4. Each device adds its own delay; earlier ranging needed a user to calibrate itEach phone adds its own unknown delay when it starts to play or record. Earlier sound-ranging systems needed a person to calibrate it away (§8). On cheap devices, the reference time between two devices could also drift by more than 50 µs a second (§3.2).
  5. Your turn Drag the warm air across the path
ToF error, peak only –
°C error, peak only –
true vs peak only

It shows The peak alone reads the ToF in steps of 5.2 µs, about 1.7 °C on this path, so it cannot follow a 1 °C change.

How to read it Time runs right; the line is the true temperature, a dot one reading of the peak alone, the faint lines the levels it lands on.

Solution 1 · OFDM phase

The correlation peak and the carrier's phase together

we combine the index of the cross-correlation peak and the phase of the peakAs a phase change of 2π at 19 kHz carrier is equivalent to 52.6 μs in ToF, we can use the cross-correlation result that has a resolution of 20.8 μs to determine how many 2π the phase has been changed.

  1. New: the carrier's phase
  2. One phase turn is 52.6 µs of ToF
  3. Both phones send: their delays cancel
  4. Peak and phase follow the warming room
  5. Your turn Phase off, drag warm air

we can achieve a ToF accuracy of 0.371μsBy removing the ambiguity of phase measurement using the coarse-grained correlation results, we can achieve a ToF accuracy of 0.371μs, which is enough to capture temperature change of 0.12 °C along a 60 cm path.

ToF error vs true paper 0.371 µs, 50 cm–
°C error vs true –

the correlation peaks corresponding to paths with close ToF will mergeWhat is left: the phase does not fix this. An echo under 30 cm longer than the direct path merges with its peak. The paper's ways out: wider bandwidth and longer frames, or leaving out the paths that merge.

the correlation peak

It shows Odd tones carry phone A's code and even tones phone B's, so each frame gives both peaks, and each peak's phase gives the fine part.

How to read it Top right: the 17–21 kHz band; left: the CIR's height against the sample number; right: the peak's phase, one turn for each 52.6 µs.

temperature read

It shows With the phase added, the reading follows the true temperature instead of jumping between the peak's levels.

How to read it The line is the true temperature; a large dot is a reading by peak and phase, a faint dot one by the peak alone.

Challenge 2 · Radon mismatch

Travel time sums the inverse speed, not the temperature

traditional Radon transform cannot be directly applied to our problem

The distribution information is completely lost in this case.

  1. A phone and a line of microphones turn around the area
  2. Each path's travel time sums the inverse speed along it
  3. Back-projecting the travel times themselves loses the hot square
  4. Our simulation: the map's hottest point stays mid-area
  5. Your turn Drag the hot square
hot square (x, y) –
map's hottest point (x, y) –
true and rebuilt field

It shows Back-projecting the ToF itself loses the field (the paper, Fig. 6(a)); in our simulation the hottest point stays mid-area.

How to read it Left: the true field, the square ringed; middle: one over the back-projected ToF, its hottest point ringed; right: each path's ToF at this angle.

Solution 2 · dRadon

dRadon: back-projecting the change in time of flight

dRadon back-projects each path's change in ToF, which is linear in the warming along it.We call this differential form of temperature changes as the dRadon transform, which has a similar formulation as the original Radon transform.

  1. New: each path's ToF change from the 20 °C room
  2. That change grows with the warming along the path
  3. Smoothed, spread to 360 angles, added up: the square
  4. Your turn dRadon off and on, drag the hot square

On the paper's turning platform, this rebuilt the field to about a decimeter.Therefore, our ToF measurements are accurate enough to reconstruct the temperature distribution at a decimeter-level resolution.

map's typical °C error –

In most of real-world scenarios, we cannot rotate the acoustic devicesWhat is left: this page turns its microphones round the area, as a lab can. A car cannot be scanned so; the next challenge starts there.

true and rebuilt field

It shows dRadon adds up each path's change in ToF, not the ToF, so the hot square comes back in its place.

How to read it The true field (square ringed), the rebuilt one (hottest point ringed), the ToF changes of 36 × 20 paths, then 18 angles without filling in.

Challenge 3 · Few devices

A few devices cannot give paths at every angle

In real-world scenarios, we cannot get the acoustic paths in all desired angles with a small number of devices.

  1. One pair: Device A at the front, Device B at the backThe paper (Sec. 4.5): extra devices “could incur formidable cost when the wiring cost is non-negligible”, as in a car.
  2. The direct path crosses the seats unevenly
  3. Four close mics give four near-same paths: the seats look alike
  4. The seats' error stays large
  5. Your turn Drag the warm air from seat to seat
seat error, direct paths –
the four seats

It shows One pair gives paths at few angles: four mics, four near-same direct paths through two seats, so the four seats look alike.

How to read it Left, each seat's true air and its estimate; middle, the seats from above, front to the left; right, each direct path's metres in each seat.

Solution 3 · Reflections

Reflected paths and a model trained once

different paths pass through the cells, i.e., the four seats, in different waysThus, the number of paths is much larger than the number of cells and the linear equations are often over-determined.

  1. New: echoes off the car's windows
  2. Each echo is a later peak: a longer path
  3. A trained model turns ToF changes into seats
  4. Your turn Echoes off and on, drag the warm seat

Weights learned once turn the paths' ToF changes into the four seats' temperatures.We solve this linear regression problem by the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) method or Ridge regression depending on the scenarios.

seat error paper 0.44 °C, 2 cars–

the variance of the errors is very largeWhat is left: the error's spread, up to 2 to 3 °C in the paper, its mean about 0.5 °C. Here the cabin, its echoes and the training frames are assumed, so the run's error shows the idea, not the paper's numbers.

the car's CIR

It shows Each echo is a later peak, the same at 5 °C and 15 °C; the table gives each path's metres in each seat.

How to read it Left: peak height against path length in metres, at 5 and 15 °C; right: one mic's paths by seat, rows of the linear model.

the four seats

It shows With the echoes, many paths cross the seats in different ways, so the trained model tells the four seats apart.

How to read it Each seat has two bars: its true air temperature and the estimate from the paths.

Limits §7: laborious training, one-place weights, wind avoided, close reflections, noise, error spread.Training needs days of warmed seats; the weights fit one place only; the tests avoided wind; close reflections and wideband noise disturb readings; errors spread up to 2–3 °C. Check the Paper · 2 of 3

Ablation study

Question What does each part of VECTOR add to its accuracy?Each part answers one challenge of the paper. A tab tests its parts where they matter: two phones 60 cm apart, the simulated field of Fig. 6, a car with one warm seat. Every try stays in the chart.

You change
VECTOR's parts, one off at a time
Time of flightTemperature mapSeats in a car
  1. 1Your turn Drop the carrier phase.Without the phase only the correlation peak is left, in steps of 5.2 μs, while 1 °C moves the ToF by 3 μs on this path.
  2. 2Your turn Stop two-way timing.Each phone adds an unknown delay to what it plays and records. Both phones play and both record: the paper's Eq. 6 adds the phase each hears of its own sound and takes away the two heard across, so the delays cancel (§3.4). Without it they stay in.
  3. 3Your turn Press All on.VECTOR as the paper runs it: the peak counts the whole cycles, the phase gives the rest.
error at 60 cm, this try –
error at 60 cm, all on –

What you saw Error: the mean gap between the path's air and VECTOR's reading over 200 frames. The phones' delays are up to 50 ms each (assumed); the phase noise is sized to the paper's 0.371 μs.fine-grained phase estimation achieves submicrosecond time resolution using the phase of the carrier frequency at 19 kHz we choose to cancel the unknown delays by obtaining reciprocal measurements from both devices The average temperature error of VECTOR is smaller than 0.25 °C and the maximum error is less than 0.9 °C under different room temperatures.

  1. 1Your turn Press dRadon off.The ToF adds up how slow the sound is along the path, not the temperature. Back-projecting the ToF and taking the reciprocal, as Fig. 6(a) does, loses the field.
  2. 2Your turn Leave sinogram gaps.With 18 scan angles, the gaps between them leave phantom lines (Fig. 6(b)). Filling the sinogram in along the angles makes the map more accurate (Fig. 6(c)).
  3. 3Your turn Press All on.dRadon with the sinogram filled in: the hot square comes back in its place.
map error, this try –
map error, all on –

What you saw Error: the RMS gap between the map and the field over a 40 × 40 cm grid. The field is Fig. 5's: 50 °C in a 20 °C circle, 0 °C round it; its sizes are assumed.The distribution information is completely lost in this case. we need to perform interpolation on the sinogram to improve the accuracy VECTOR can measure the temperature on the LOS path with an error of 0.25 °C and reconstruct the temperature distribution with a decimeter-level spatial resolution

  1. 1Your turn Keep only straight paths.One pair of devices gives each microphone one direct path, and here they cross the right seats only. A seat no path crosses cannot be read.
  2. 2Your turn Press All on.The direct paths and the echoes off the cabin, each crossing the seats in its own way, read all four seats.

What you saw Error: the four seats' mean gap to their sensors, front-left seat 5 °C warmer. The cabin, the devices' places and the windows are assumed, fitted to the path lengths of Fig. 9.we cannot get the acoustic paths in all desired angles with a small number of devices VECTOR achieves an average temperature error of 0.44 °C for temperature reconstruction of four seats in two different cars with one pair of transceivers.

Generalization study

Question How far past its tests does VECTOR keep reading the air?The paper tests two phones in 7 to 28 °C rooms (§6.3, Fig. 11(a)), 30 to 150 cm apart at 14 to 16 °C (Fig. 11(b)), and maps with 36 scan angles (Sec. 4.4). Here: 10 cm to 5 m, −20 to 50 °C, 6 to 72 angles.

You change
the distance, the warm air, the scan angles
DistanceWarm airScan angles
  1. 1Your turn Slide the distance (try 3 m).A longer path gives more microseconds per degree, but a weaker peak. In the model, past about 3 m the peak's jitter nears half a carrier cycle and whole cycles start to slip: the mean error jumps while the median holds.
  2. 2Your turn Drag the hot area off the path.Only the air the sound crosses counts: off the path, the reading falls back to the room's.

What you saw The room is 15 °C, as in Fig. 11(b); the hot area is ours. The model's signal-to-noise ratio falls as 1/distance from 30 dB at 50 cm (assumed); its phase noise is sized to Fig. 10. The paper's medians are read off Fig. 11(b).VECTOR can reliably measure the temperature when the devices are separated by 30 cm to 150 cm with room temperatures of 14 ∼ 16 °C

  1. 1Your turn Slide the hot area's rise (try +40 °C).dRadon and the seats' model treat a path's travel-time change as a straight line in the temperature, dropping the higher terms (Sec. 4.3.1). Indoors that is safe: sound speeds up by under 10 m/s, a rise under about 16 °C. The part dropped grows faster than the rise.
  2. 2Your turn Slide the room's warmth (try −20 °C).Sound is 12 % slower at −20 °C than at 50 °C; the pair reads that speed as a temperature. In the cars (−1.9 to 46.2 °C, §6.4) the paper's error rises to about 2 °C when hot, possibly from the phone overheating above 30 °C (Fig. 14(b)): not modelled.

What This Model Leaves Open

Not modelled

Shown by the paper, not simulated here.

  1. Two more uses: feedback for a data centre's cooling (b), and a smart home's rooms (c)The model builds the car and the paper's test set-ups only; these two uses are seen in the authors' talk on the first page, not simulated. §2.2, Fig. 1(b), Fig. 1(c)
  2. Heat sources told apart (none, an air conditioner, a radiator heater) by the low- and high-frequency energy of the readingsTelling heat sources apart is a classifier trained on measured readings; the model simulates no source's own pattern of change, so it has nothing to classify. §6.6, Fig. 18
  3. The time to process a 40 ms frame: 0.494 ms on an iPhone 6S, 10.841 ms on a Samsung S7, 16.731 ms on a Raspberry Pi 3B+Run time on phones and a Raspberry Pi: the model runs in the reader's browser, so it cannot time those devices. §6.7, Table 1
  4. Who hears the 17–21 kHz signal: 3 of 18 men and 1 of 12 womenA study of people's hearing: the model plays no sound and has no listener. §6.7.2, Table 2
  5. Carrier frequency: kept at the paper's 19 kHzleft at the paper's 19 kHz: its 17 to 21 kHz band is one most people do not hear (Sec. 3.5), and the paper tests no other carrier §3.1; Sec. 3.5; §6.1
  6. Frame length: kept at the paper's 40 ms (160 ms in the car)left at the paper's 40 ms, and 160 ms in the car, where the longer frame lets reflections on longer paths be caught (§6.4); the model finds each path's time of flight without frames §6.1; §6.4
  7. Which car: one cabin for the paper's twoone cabin, assumed: the devices stand alike in the paper's two cars (Fig. 13(c) draws car 1), and the cars differ in their reflections, from their structure and interior, which the model does not take apart §6.4, Fig. 13(c), Fig. 14
  8. The kind of heat source: one still warm spot, not how it changes over timeleft at one still spot of warmer air: the paper tells a room without heating, an air conditioner and a radiator heater apart by how the temperature varies over time (Fig. 18), which the model's still field does not have §6.6, Fig. 18
